name: Oksapmin
sweep_summary: Oksapmin is not in the catalog. The single sweep hit, Lawrence 1977 'Verb morphology and discourse prosodies' (SIL Workpapers 20:143-148), was obtained (Wayback copy of the SIL archive PDF; scanned, no text layer) and read in full: it is a Tagmemic argument that tense/mood suffixes belong to sentence/discourse structure; 'prosodies' means discourse-level abstracted features, and the only phonological remark is sentence-final falling intonation vs medial phrase pitch. Silent on word stress. Sweep also recovered Lawrence 1993 Oksapmin dictionary 'Grammar Notes' (Wayback copy of SIL archive PDF, scanned): sec. 3.3 Pitch, p. 209, gives two contrasting word-level pitch melodies (high-falling vs low-rising; glides on monosyllables) plus phrase pitch peaking on new information, with no mention of stress. Loughnane 2009 (already on file, re-read: sec. 2.1.5, pp. 62-63) finds no word-level suprasegmentals and no stress, pitch operating only at intonational-phrase level, and explicitly rejects Lawrence's word-pitch analysis. One first-hand source could not be obtained: Lawrence 1992 'Oksapmin Organised Phonology Data' (4 pp., SIL archive 42223), blocked by Cloudflare on the live URL with no Wayback snapshot; priority high as the likeliest direct stress/suprasegmental statement. Internet Archive CDX was intermittently offline; all fetched sources pages/PDFs and are under

new_statements.quote: I have not found any evidence for the existence of any suprasegmentals associated with the syllable or word which are contrastive in Oksapmin. Heavier syllables or syllables which contain a vowel which is inherently longer, particularly /a/, may sound stressed or prominent (see e.g. Cruttenden 1997) to the English speaker but I have found no language internal evidence to suggest that stress is a suprasegmental feature. Pitch and intensity are correlated and peak at each syllable nucleus. Pitch variation does, however, operate beyond the domain of the word in a delimiting function, see §2.7 for details.
new_statements.citation: Loughnane, Robyn. 2009. A Grammar of Oksapmin. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne, sec. 2.1.5 Suprasegmentals, pp. 62-63.
new_statements.reading: Oksapmin has no word stress: the only full grammar finds no word-level or syllable-level contrastive suprasegmentals, treats impressions of prominence on heavy /a/ syllables as an English-listener artefact, and locates all pitch variation at the intonational-phrase level. The only first-hand counter-analysis is Lawrence 1993:209 (dictionary grammar notes, fetched sources and scanned this sweep), which posits two contrasting word-level pitch melodies (high-falling vs low-rising) but says nothing about stress; Loughnane cites and rejects it (fn. 10). Lawrence 1977, the sweep's title hit, is silent on word stress (its 'prosodies' are Tagmemic discourse-level abstractions; only sentence-final falling intonation is mentioned). Net: no dominant stress pattern to code; if coded at all, 'no word stress' (Loughnane) with the Lawrence word-pitch analysis as the recorded variant.

sources.citation: Loughnane, Robyn. 2009. A Grammar of Oksapmin. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne. Sec. 2.1.5 Suprasegmentals (pp. 62-63); sec. 2.7 The Intonational Phrase (pp. 78-85).
sources.quote: I have not found any evidence for the existence of any suprasegmentals associated with the syllable or word which are contrastive in Oksapmin. Heavier syllables or syllables which contain a vowel which is inherently longer, particularly /a/, may sound stressed or prominent (see e.g. Cruttenden 1997) to the English speaker but I have found no language internal evidence to suggest that stress is a suprasegmental feature. Pitch and intensity are correlated and peak at each syllable nucleus. Pitch variation does, however, operate beyond the domain of the word in a delimiting function, see §2.7 for details. [pp. 62-63]
sources.note: No word stress and no contrastive word-level suprasegmentals; pitch and intensity peak on every syllable nucleus; pitch works only at the intonational-phrase level (downdrift, final fall in isolation words and statements, sustained/rising pitch on medial verbs). Footnote 10 explicitly contrasts this with Lawrence 1993:209's two-word-pitch analysis. Also notes (sec. 2.1) that Oksapmin has no suprasegmental phonemes 'unlike some neighbouring languages, e.g. Mian'.

sources.citation: Lawrence, Marshall. 1977. "Verb morphology and discourse prosodies." In Richard Loving & David Thomas (eds), Proceedings of the S.I.L. consultants seminar, Ukarumpa 1976, 143-148. Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 20. Ukarumpa: SIL.
sources.quote: The period at the end of example (1) represents falling intonation, which contrasts with phrase pitch medially. [p. 143] ... Briefly, tense and mood terminate a structural unit, which then relates to a structural unit following it in the discourse; falling intonation terminates a unit of information in which the last item of the unit receives prominence. [p. 146]
sources.locator: pp. 143 and 146 (6-page paper read in full)
sources.note: Nothing about word stress or word accent. Despite the title, 'prosodies' is used in the Tagmemic sense: tense/mood and 'specificness' abstracted as discourse-level features. The only phonological prosody mentioned is sentence-final falling intonation versus medial phrase pitch. The SIL archive subjects are 'Verb Morphology; Intonation'. Silent on stress placement.

sources.citation: Lawrence, Marshall (comp.). 1993. Oksapmin dictionary. Dictionaries of Papua New Guinea 13. Ukarumpa: SIL. Appendix 'Grammar Notes', sec. 3.3 Pitch (p. 209) and 3.4 Intonation (p. 210).
sources.quote: 3.3 Pitch. Words have one of two contrasting pitches: high initially, dropping to mid on the last syllable, then falling; or low initially rising to mid on the last syllable. On monosyllable words these are glides: high-mid or low-mid. [p. 209] As well as contrastive word pitch, Oksapmin has phrase pitch. Phrase pitch has one high pitch peak for each unit. A pitch unit signals an information unit with the pitch peaking on the informationally new item in the unit. [p. 210]
sources.locator: Appendix Grammar Notes, sec. 3.3 Pitch, p. 209; sec. 3.4 Intonation, p. 210
sources.note: First-hand SIL fieldworker's word-prosody statement: two contrasting word-level pitch melodies (an implicit pitch-accent/tone analysis), plus phrase-level pitch peaks on new information. The phonology notes (alphabet, vowel length, pitch, intonation, pp. 208-210) never mention stress or accent, so no stress-placement rule is given. This is the analysis Loughnane 2009 (fn. 10, p. 62) quotes and rejects, and the source of Wikipedia's 'two tones' claim.

sources.note: Not read. The file is openly posted by SIL but the download URL sits behind a Cloudflare JS challenge from our machine (curl, curl_cffi impersonation, headless Chrome and web lookups all get 403 'Just a moment'), and there is no Wayback snapshot of the PDF. SIL Organised Phonology Data sheets normally carry an explicit suprasegmental/stress section, so this 4-page sheet is the likeliest place for a direct first-hand statement on Oksapmin stress by the Lawrences.
